sections.content:
In Class IX, you began your exploration of the world of real numbers and encountered irrational numbers. We continue our discussion on real numbers in this chapter. We begin with very important properties of positive integers in Sections 1.2, namely the Euclid’s division algorithm and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

Euclid’s division algorithm, as the name suggests, has to do with divisibility of integers. Stated simply, it says any positive integer $a$ can be divided by another positive integer $b$ in such a way that it leaves a remainder $r$ that is smaller than $b$. Many of you probably recognise this as the usual long division process. Although this result is quite easy to state and understand, it has many applications related to the divisibility properties of integers. We touch upon a few of them, and use it mainly to compute the HCF of two positive integers.

The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, on the other hand, has to do something with multiplication of positive integers. You already know that every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes in a unique way—this important fact is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Again, while it is a result that is easy to state and understand, it has some very deep and significant applications in the field of mathematics. We use the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic for two main applications. First, we use it to prove the irrationality of many of the numbers you studied in Class IX, such as $\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$ and $\sqrt{5}$. Second, we apply this theorem to explore when exactly the decimal expansion of a rational number, say $\frac{p}{q} (q \neq 0)$, is terminating and when it is non-terminating repeating. We do so by looking at the prime factorisation of the denominator $q$ of $\frac{p}{q}$. You will see that the prime factorisation of $q$ will completely reveal the nature of the decimal expansion of $\frac{p}{q}$.

So let us begin our exploration.

segments.text: Welcome back to the world of real numbers! In Class 9, you explored irrational numbers. Now, we are going to dive deeper into two powerful properties of positive integers: division and multiplication.

First, let's look at division through Euclid's division algorithm. It simply says that if you divide a positive integer 'a' by another positive integer 'b', you get a remainder 'r' that is always smaller than 'b'. Let me show you [https://gradeup-books-images.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/avatar-visuals/cbse/10/maths/unit-1/introduction_explain_1_a1cea1c8ad.jpg]. Look at how dividing objects into equal groups always leaves a remainder smaller than the size of one group! You might recognize this as the long division you already know, and we will use it mainly to find the Highest Common Factor, or HCF, of two numbers.

segments.text: Next, let's talk about multiplication and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. This theorem states that every composite number can be written as a product of prime numbers in a completely unique way. Let me show you [https://gradeup-books-images.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/avatar-visuals/cbse/10/maths/unit-1/introduction_explain_2_6e6bacef0c.jpg]. Notice how breaking a number down into its prime building blocks gives a single, unique result no matter how you start!

segments.text: We will use this multiplication theorem for two huge tasks. First, to prove that numbers like the square root of 2, 3, and 5 are irrational. Second, by looking at the prime factors of the denominator 'q' in a fraction p/q, we can easily tell if its decimal form terminates or repeats forever.

Now, let's return to our starting question! When you pack 17 apples into bags of 5, you fill 3 full bags using 15 apples. That leaves 2 apples leftover. Since 2 is smaller than the bag size of 5, the correct option is A!

sections.content:
In your earlier classes, you have seen that any natural number can be written as a product of its prime factors. For instance, $2 = 2$, $4 = 2 \times 2$, $253 = 11 \times 23$, and so on. Now, let us try and look at natural numbers from the other direction. That is, can any natural number be obtained by multiplying prime numbers? Let us see.

Take any collection of prime numbers, say 2, 3, 7, 11 and 23. If we multiply some or all of these numbers, allowing them to repeat as many times as we wish, we can produce a large collection of positive integers (In fact, infinitely many). Let us list a few :

$$7 \times 11 \times 23 = 1771$$

$$3 \times 7 \times 11 \times 23 = 5313$$

$$2 \times 3 \times 7 \times 11 \times 23 = 10626$$

$$2^3 \times 3 \times 7^3 = 8232$$

$$2^2 \times 3 \times 7 \times 11 \times 23 = 21252$$

and so on.

Now, let us suppose your collection of primes includes all the possible primes. What is your guess about the size of this collection? Does it contain only a finite number of integers, or infinitely many? In fact, there are infinitely many primes. So, if we combine all these primes in all possible ways, we will get an infinite

collection of numbers, all the primes and all possible products of primes. The question is – can we produce all the composite numbers this way? What do you think? Do you think that there may be a composite number which is not the product of powers of primes? Before we answer this, let us factorise positive integers, that is, do the opposite of what we have done so far.

We are going to use the factor tree with which you are all familiar. Let us take some large number, say, 32760, and factorise it as shown.
![img-1.jpeg](https://gradeup-books-images.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/structured-content/cbse/10/maths/unit-1/img-1.jpeg)

So we have factorised 32760 as $2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13$ as a product of primes, i.e., $32760 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13$ as a product of powers of primes. Let us try another number, say, 123456789. This can be written as $3^2 \times 3803 \times 3607$. Of course, you have to check that 3803 and 3607 are primes! (Try it out for several other natural numbers yourself.) This leads us to a conjecture that every composite number can be written as the product of powers of primes. In fact, this statement is true, and is called the **Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic** because of its basic crucial importance to the study of integers. Let us now formally state this theorem.

section_enrichment.concept_overview: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic states that every composite number can be broken down into a unique product of prime numbers, regardless of the order in which they are written. This unique breakdown allows us to easily compute the Highest Common Factor (HCF) and Least Common Multiple (LCM) of positive integers.

faqs.question: What is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic?
faqs.answer: It states that every composite number can be uniquely expressed as a product of prime numbers, regardless of the order of factors.

faqs.question: Does HCF × LCM = Product of numbers work for three numbers?
faqs.answer: No, the relationship HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b holds true only for two positive integers, not for three or more.

faqs.question: Who proved the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic?
faqs.answer: While Euclid recorded a version of it in Euclid's Elements, Carl Friedrich Gauss gave the first correct proof in his work Disquisitiones Arithmeticae.

phases.scenario: Imagine you are building a number using prime factor blocks: three blocks of 2 and two blocks of 3. If you multiply them all together, what single composite number do you construct?

option_explanations.B: Not quite! That would be two 2s and two 3s (2² × 3² = 4 × 9 = 36), missing one factor of 2.

option_explanations.D: Not quite! That would be two 2s and three 3s (2² × 3³ = 4 × 27 = 108), swapping the count of 2s and 3s.

A.text: You predicted 72! Spot on—every combination of prime factors builds one unique composite number.

B.text: You predicted 36. Don't worry, forgetting one exponent factor is a classic slip!

C.text: You predicted 12. Remember, we multiply the factors together rather than adding them!

D.text: You predicted 108. Swapping the prime powers is easy to do, but order of exponents changes the product!

segments.text: Welcome! We already know how to break numbers down into prime factors, like writing twenty-five as five times five. But what happens if we look at it from the other direction and build composite numbers by multiplying prime numbers together?

If we collect prime numbers and multiply them in different combinations, we can generate every single composite number! Let's see how a large number like 32,760 breaks down. [https://gradeup-books-images.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/avatar-visuals/cbse/10/maths/unit-1/the_fundamental_theorem_of_ari_explain_1_332348e903.jpg] Look at how this factor tree breaks 32,760 down into two cubed times three squared times five times seven times thirteen. This gives us the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every composite number has a completely unique set of prime factors! Euclid first recorded an early version of this, and Carl Friedrich Gauss later gave the first complete proof.

visual.prompt: a chalkboard displaying a step-by-step factor tree branching down from the number 32760 into prime factors at the bottom
visual.planned_because: the teaching writer placed it here

segments.text: This uniqueness is super powerful! For example, take the expression four to the power of n. Could this ever end in the digit zero? For a number to end in zero, its prime factors must include five. But four to the power of n is just two raised to two n, meaning two is its only prime factor. By our uniqueness rule, five can never appear, so four to the power of n will never end in zero!

We can also use prime factorisation to quickly find the HCF and LCM of numbers. [https://gradeup-books-images.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/avatar-visuals/cbse/10/maths/unit-1/the_fundamental_theorem_of_ari_explain_2_08bd6d0b8c.jpg] Look at how we arrange these prime powers. The HCF is the product of the smallest power of each common prime factor, while the LCM takes the greatest power of every prime factor involved! Plus, for any two positive integers, multiplying their HCF and LCM gives the exact same result as multiplying the two numbers together.

visual.prompt: a wooden tabletop with prime number blocks arranged in groups showing the common smallest powers and all greatest powers
visual.planned_because: the teaching writer placed it here

segments.text: Keep in mind one important detail! This neat formula where HCF times LCM equals the product of the numbers only works for two numbers. It does not work when you have three numbers, like six, seventy-two, and one hundred twenty!

Now, let's return to our starting question! We wanted to find the composite number built from three blocks of two and two blocks of three. Calculating two cubed gives eight, and three squared gives nine. Multiplying eight by nine gives seventy-two, making option A the correct answer!

reveal.text: By breaking 6 into 2 × 3 and 20 into 2² × 5, we take the highest powers of all prime factors: 2² × 3 × 5 = 60. So both buses arrive together every 60 minutes!

interaction.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Look at the common prime factor 2: its powers are 2⁵ in 96 and 2² in 404. Take the smallest power, 2²!

pool.title: The Ending Zero Mystery
pool.question: Can 4ⁿ ever end with the digit 0 for any natural number n? Why or why not?

ask.text: Look closely at this picture. Can 4ⁿ ever end with the digit 0 for any natural number n? Why or why not?

options.A: No, because its prime factorisation only has 2s, and a prime factor of 5 is required to end in 0.
options.B: Yes, because as n gets large enough, 4ⁿ will eventually end in 0.
options.C: No, because 4 is an even number, and numbers ending in 0 must be odd.

option_explanations.A: Yeah, you got the right answer! For a number to end in 0, it must be divisible by 10, meaning its prime factorisation must contain both 2 and 5. Since 4ⁿ = (2²)ⁿ = 2²ⁿ, the only prime factor is 2.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect! By the uniqueness part of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, no new prime factor like 5 can ever appear in 4ⁿ no matter how large n gets.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect! Numbers ending in 0 (like 10, 20, 30) are actually even, not odd.

reveal.text: Because 4ⁿ contains only the prime factor 2, and the uniqueness theorem guarantees no other prime factors exist, it can never contain 5 and thus can never end in 0!

Also, for any two numbers, their product equals the product of their HCF and LCM!

sections.content:
In Class IX, you were introduced to irrational numbers and many of their properties. You studied about their existence and how the rationals and the irrationals together made up the real numbers. You even studied how to locate irrationals on the number line. However, we did not prove that they were irrationals. In this section, we will prove that $\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}, \sqrt{5}$ and, in general, $\sqrt{p}$ is irrational, where $p$ is a prime. One of the theorems, we use in our proof, is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

Recall, a number 's' is called *irrational* if it cannot be written in the form $\frac{p}{q}$, where $p$ and $q$ are integers and $q \neq 0$. Some examples of irrational numbers, with which you are already familiar, are :

$$\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}, \sqrt{15}, \pi, -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}, 0.10110111011110 \dots, \text{etc.}$$

Before we prove that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational, we need the following theorem, whose proof is based on the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

section_enrichment.concept_overview: This lesson explains how to prove that square roots of prime numbers are irrational using proof by contradiction and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

faqs.question: What is proof by contradiction?
faqs.answer: It is a mathematical proof method where you assume the opposite of what you want to prove, show that it leads to an impossible situation or contradiction, and conclude that your original statement must be true.

faqs.question: What does it mean for two numbers to be coprime?
faqs.answer: Two numbers are coprime if their only common positive factor is 1.

faqs.question: Does Theorem 1.2 work if p is not a prime number?
faqs.answer: No, p must be a prime number. For example, 4 divides 6 squared (36), but 4 does not divide 6.

segments.text: Welcome back! Today, we are going to learn how to prove that numbers like the square root of 2 or square root of 3 are actually irrational.

Remember, an irrational number is one that cannot be written as a fraction a over b, where a and b are integers. To prove a number is irrational, we use a clever technique called proof by contradiction. Let me show you [https://gradeup-books-images.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/avatar-visuals/cbse/10/maths/unit-1/revisiting_irrational_numbers_explain_1_d2f3306e5b.jpg]. We start by assuming the exact opposite—that the number IS rational!

segments.text: Before we prove square root of 2 is irrational, we need an important rule. If a prime number p divides a squared, then p MUST also divide a. This rule comes directly from the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic because prime factors are unique.

Now, let me show you how we use this to test square root of 2 [https://gradeup-books-images.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/avatar-visuals/cbse/10/maths/unit-1/revisiting_irrational_numbers_explain_2_960e9b9bdc.jpg]. If square root of 2 were a over b, where a and b share no common factors, then squaring both sides gives 2 times b squared equals a squared. This means 2 divides a squared, so 2 must divide a!

visual.prompt: a classroom blackboard with mathematical equations neatly written in white chalk showing square root of 2 equals a over b
visual.planned_because: the teaching writer placed it here

segments.text: If 2 divides a, we can write a as 2 times c. Substituting this back gives b squared equals 2 times c squared, which means 2 ALSO divides b! But wait, we said a and b had no common factors, and now both are divisible by 2. That is a contradiction, which proves our starting assumption was wrong, so square root of 2 must be irrational!

We can use this exact same method for numbers like 5 minus square root of 3 or 3 times square root of 2. By rearranging the equation to isolate the irrational root on one side, we get a rational number equal to an irrational one, which is impossible!
Back to our opening question! Since 5 is a prime number, if 5 divides a squared, then by Theorem 1.2, 5 MUST also divide the original integer a. So the correct option is A!

pool.title: The Coprime Confusion
pool.question: A student writes 3b² = a² and concludes that both 'a' and 'b' are divisible by 3. Why does this create a contradiction if a/b was assumed to be in simplest form?

ask.text: Look closely at this picture. A student writes 3b² = a² and concludes that both 'a' and 'b' are divisible by 3. Why does this create a contradiction if a/b was assumed to be in simplest form?

options.A: Because coprime integers 'a' and 'b' cannot share any common factor other than 1.
options.B: Because 3 is not a prime number.
options.C: Because 'a' and 'b' must both be odd numbers.

option_explanations.A: Yeah, you got the right answer! If 'a' and 'b' share 3 as a common factor, they were not coprime, contradicting our original assumption.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect, 3 is indeed a prime number.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect, being odd or even is not the core contradiction here.

reveal.text: Since 'a' and 'b' were assumed to be coprime, finding that 3 divides both of them creates a contradiction, proving √3 cannot be rational!

key_points: Assume √2 is rational and write it as a/b where a and b are coprime integers.
Square both sides to get 2b² = a², showing that 2 divides a², so 2 divides a.
Substitute a = 2c to show 2b² = 4c², meaning b² = 2c², so 2 divides b.
Conclude that 2 divides both a and b, contradicting that a and b are coprime.
phases.model_explanation: To prove √2 is irrational, we assume the opposite: that √2 is rational and equals a/b, where a and b are coprime integers. Squaring both sides gives 2b² = a², which means 2 divides a², so 2 must divide a. We can write a = 2c. Substituting this back gives b² = 2c², meaning 2 also divides b. This contradicts our assumption that a and b have no common factors other than 1. Thus, √2 must be irrational.
phases.guidance: A good explanation states the definition in plain words, shows the procedure on a tiny example of the student's own, names the key property (order, count, the empty case) and the common mistake to avoid.
